client: I've been really struggling lately with everything piling up at work. They just handed me this massive project with a deadline that feels impossible, and half my team is out, so I'm basically trying to do everything myself. Honestly, I'm not even sure talking about it is going to change anything, because the work is still going to be there when I leave this office.
therapist: What you're carrying right now sounds genuinely exhausting - an impossible deadline, a depleted team, and the weight of feeling like it all falls on you. I also notice a kind of quiet resignation in how you're speaking about this, like you're worn down not just by the workload, but by a sense of hopelessness that anything could shift. You're right that the work will still be there, but I wonder if we could explore whether the story you're telling yourself about having to handle *everything* alone is fully accurate, or if that belief might actually be adding to the burden.
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, moderate-paced speech

client: I hear what you're saying, and part of me wants to agree with you, but honestly it kind of frustrates me a little. Like, it's not just a story I'm telling myself - my manager literally said "figure it out" and walked away, and two of my team members are out sick. I don't know how to separate the belief from the reality when the reality actually is that bad.
therapist: You're absolutely right to push back on that, and I'm glad you did - the frustration in your voice tells me that felt dismissive of what's a very real, very concrete situation, and I don't want to minimize that. Your manager's response was genuinely unhelpful, your team members are actually out, and those are facts, not distortions. What I'm curious about, though, is whether within that very real pressure, there might be any small degree of flexibility - like what "figuring it out" could look like that doesn't require you to do everything perfectly and alone.
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, fast speech

client: I guess... when you put it that way, maybe there is a small part of me that automatically goes to "I have to handle all of this perfectly or I've failed." But it's hard to separate that from the reality that the work genuinely does need to get done, and I'm the only one there to do it. I just don't know what "not perfectly" even looks like when there are actual deadlines and a manager who's already watching me.
therapist: There's something really significant in what you just noticed - that automatic pull toward "perfect or failed" - and even though your words are measured and thoughtful, the tension in your voice tells me this is hitting somewhere deeper and more urgent than you might be letting on. "Not perfectly" in a real deadline situation might look like prioritizing the two or three things that matter most and letting some things be *good enough* rather than flawless - which isn't failure, it's actually a strategic decision. I wonder what your manager would actually notice or care about, versus what the perfectionist part of you is convinced they'll scrutinize?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, loud, fast speech

client: Honestly, my manager would probably just care that the report is done and hits the key numbers — I know that logically. But the perfectionist part of me is convinced that if there's even one awkward sentence or a formatting inconsistency, she's going to think less of me, like it'll undo all the good work I've done before. And I guess what scares me is that I can't fully trust my own judgment about what "good enough" actually looks like, because my bar for myself is so high that I've kind of lost perspective on what's normal.
therapist: The way you just said that - quietly, almost carefully, like you were admitting something vulnerable - matches exactly what you're describing: a part of you that's been holding itself to an exhausting standard for so long that "normal" has genuinely lost its shape. What you've just identified is really important though - you *do* know what your manager actually cares about, which means your judgment isn't broken, it's just being overridden by a fear that one imperfection will erase everything you've built. That fear deserves some gentle questioning - can you think of a time when someone you respected delivered something imperfect, and it *didn't* define how you saw all their previous work?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, very quiet, moderate-paced speech

client: I mean... yeah, I can think of examples like that with other people. My colleague Sarah once sent out a report with some pretty glaring errors in it, and I didn't suddenly think less of everything she'd done before that. But it feels completely different when it's me - like the rules just don't apply the same way, and I know that probably sounds irrational when I say it out loud.
therapist: The fact that you're speaking quickly, like the words are tumbling out ahead of you, tells me something just clicked in a way that feels both clarifying and a little unsettling - you can *hear* the double standard even as you're describing it. What you just did is actually one of the most powerful things in this kind of work: you found your own evidence, in your own life, that imperfection doesn't erase worth - and you did that, I didn't hand it to you. So I want to gently stay with that question: if the rule doesn't apply to Sarah, what would it mean to experiment - just this once, with this report - with extending yourself the same humanity you so naturally gave her?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, very rapid speech

client:
Yeah, I hear what you're saying, and part of me actually gets it in this moment... but there's this other part that immediately jumps in and says "that's different, Sarah's situation was different." Like my brain is already looking for the exit, already building the case for why I'm the exception to my own rule.

And the idea of just... letting the report be imperfect and submitting it anyway, honestly that makes my chest tighten just thinking about it. What if this is the one time the imperfection actually matters, and I've just been lucky with all the other times I told myself it was okay?
therapist: That tightness in your chest is real, and the softness in your voice right now tells me you're sitting with something genuinely scary rather than just thinking about it abstractly. But I want to reflect back what you just named so clearly: your brain is *already* searching for the exit - and noticing that pattern in real time is not a small thing, it's actually you catching the perfectionism in the act. The "what if this is the one time" thought is worth examining - because that fear has likely shown up before every other submission too, which means it's not a reliable signal that danger is actually there, it's just the alarm system that always goes off.
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, soft-spoken, moderate-paced speech

client: I hear what you're saying, and part of me gets it logically, like yeah, the alarm has gone off before and the world didn't end. But it's hard to fully believe that this time isn't different, because what if I've just been lucky so far and this is the submission where everything finally falls apart? That thought feels so convincing in the moment, even when I can see myself doing exactly what you're describing.
therapist: The way you're speaking right now - softly, carefully, like you're carrying something fragile - tells me this isn't just an intellectual puzzle for you, it's something that feels genuinely threatening in your body, even as part of you watches it happening. What you're describing has a name in CBT - it's called "what if" thinking, and its most convincing trick is that it *always* feels like this time is different, which is actually evidence that it's the pattern talking, not reality. I want to ask you something gently: across all those previous submissions where the alarm fired and the world didn't fall apart, what did you learn about your own competence - and is it possible that evidence deserves at least as much weight as the "what if"?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, soft-spoken, moderate-paced speech

client: I hear what you're saying, and part of me knows you're right - those submissions did turn out okay, mostly. But the thing is, it doesn't feel like evidence when I'm in the middle of it, it just feels like luck, like I got away with it that time but this time I might actually fail. And honestly, telling myself "it's just a pattern" while I'm spiraling doesn't really make the fear go away, it just adds this layer of frustration where I'm anxious AND annoyed at myself for being anxious.
therapist: That layer you're describing - being anxious about the anxiety, frustrated at yourself for not just *fixing* it with the right thought - is actually one of the most exhausting parts of this pattern, and the tension in your voice right now, soft but fast, tells me you're feeling that weight right now rather than just describing it. You're not failing at CBT because the fear doesn't disappear when you name it - insight and relief don't always arrive at the same time, and that's not a flaw in you. So rather than trying to think your way out of the spiral in this moment, I'm wondering - what does the anxious part of you actually need right now, not to be argued with, but to feel even slightly safer?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, soft-spoken, fast speech

client: I don't know... I think it just needs someone to tell it that it's okay to not have everything figured out right now. But even saying that feels kind of hollow, like I know that's what I'm supposed to say but I don't actually believe it. It's like there's this part of me that's convinced if I just relax my guard for one second, something will go wrong and it'll be my fault for not staying on top of it.
therapist: The softness and almost fragile quality in your voice right now tells me that what you just said cost something to admit - that the reassurance feels hollow, that you don't quite believe it yet. What you're describing underneath it is really important though: a part of you that has been standing guard for a very long time, convinced that your vigilance is the only thing standing between you and everything falling apart. I want to gently offer that the goal isn't to suddenly believe it's okay to relax - it's just to get curious about where that exhausted, watchful part of you first learned that it had to work this hard to keep you safe.
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, soft-spoken, moderate-paced speech

client: I think that part of me learned it pretty early, honestly. Growing up, things at home were unpredictable, and if I wasn't paying attention, something would go wrong and it would somehow end up being my fault. So I guess I just... never stopped paying attention, even when I grew up and moved away.
therapist: The way you just shared that - softly, almost carefully, like you were handling something delicate - tells me this is a tender place, and I want to honor how significant what you just connected is. That little child who learned to stay vigilant because the world felt unpredictable and the blame could land on them at any moment - they were doing the only thing that made sense to stay safe, and that hypervigilance was genuinely protective then. But I want to gently reflect back: you're not in that unpredictable home anymore, and part of what we might explore together is helping that younger part of you recognize that the adult you has already made it out - and maybe doesn't need to be on guard every single moment to be okay.
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, soft-spoken, moderate-paced speech
